newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Cambodian prince faces new hurdle in homecoming bid.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian prince faces new hurdle in homecoming bid.

text.p: Cambodia's national airline on Wednesday refused to fly exiled Prince Norodom Sirivudh to Phnom Penh, throwing up a new obstacle to his bid to return home to contest charges of plotting to kill co-premier Hun Sen.
"We have given firm instructions to decline any boarding of His Highness Prince Sirivudh," Royal Air Cambodge chairman Vichit Ith told Reuters in Phnom Penh, Cambodia's capital.
He said the decision was taken out of consideration for safety of other passengers.
"We do not want to take any risk," he said.
Sirivudh has been threatened with arrest if he returns to Phnom Penh, and reports from there said the government might send troops to meet any flight which carried him.

The prince, stranded in Hong Kong after Hong Kong-based carrier Dragonair refused to allow him on its Tuesday flight to Phnom Penh, told Reuters earlier he had not been hopeful of getting a seat on Royal Air Cambodge.

"I had an indication from Mr Andre Lim, the (Cambodian) consul here...that Air Cambodge will be in trouble (landing me)... It seems that we cannot even book a reservation," he said by telephone from a hotel room in Hong Kong.
The consulate was closed for a holiday and officials were unavailable for comment.
Sirivudh said on Tuesday, after flying into Hong Kong from Germany, that he would persist in attempts to go home and seek a fair trial.

A half-brother of King Norodom Sihanouk and a former foreign minister, Sirivudh went into exile in December 1995 after being held for one month on charges of involvement in an alleged plot against the life of Hun Sen.
Sirivudh said the Hong Kong government had helped his transit arrangements and provided him with security protection.
"I feel fine," he said, sounding relaxed. "I feel unhappy with Dragonair and now perhaps with Royal Cambodge, too, but not with authorities in Hong Kong."
King Sihanouk has refused to grant Sirivudh an amnesty for fear of making an enemy of Hun Sen and said he would abdicate immediately if the Sirivudh affair was settled by violence.

Strongman Hun Sen, who rules in uneasy coalition with the royalist FUNCINPEC party of Sirivudh's nephew co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh, has refused to back calls for an amnesty and last week warned of violence if the prince returned.
Last December Hun Sen said that he would shoot down any plane carrying Sirivudh.
